Laurence Humphrey
lor'ens hum'fre
n. (Laurence Humphrey, c. 1527–1589, Marian exile, President of Magdalen College, Oxford)
Latin Laurentius, crowned with laurel; Germanic Hunfrid, peace of the Hun, giant-peace.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Laurence Humphrey was a Cambridge fellow who left England when Mary Tudor came to the throne, spent the years of exile at Zurich, Basel and Geneva, and came home at Elizabeth's accession to spend the rest of his life as President of Magdalen College, Oxford, and in the end Dean of Winchester. He is remembered chiefly for what he would not do. With Thomas Sampson he refused to wear the surplice and the square cap, holding that garments borrowed from the Roman mass could not be made indifferent by an act of state, and he was disciplined for it while the vestiarian controversy ran its course. The dictionary does not treat that quarrel as a matter of taste. Humphrey's argument was that a church which had buried the mass should not keep its clothes, and that a conscience bound by Scripture cannot be unbound by a royal injunction. He also wrote the first life of Bishop Jewel and a treatise on nobility which located true greatness in godliness rather than blood, and he filled Magdalen with preachers. He was a scholar who had seen the Reformed churches of the Rhine at close quarters and never afterward thought England had gone far enough.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines exile as banishment, and nonconformity as refusal of compliance with an established usage.

expand to see more

EX'ILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country.

NONCONFORM'ITY, n. Neglect or failure of conformity; in England, the refusal to unite with the established church.

PRES'IDENT, n. An officer appointed to preside over a college or society.

CON'SCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge; the faculty, power or principle which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our actions.

Key Scripture

Act 5:29 — "Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men."

Rom 14:23 — "And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin."

1Co 10:31 — "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God."

2Co 1:12 — "For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward."

Modern Corruption

He would not wear the mass vestments, and said a conscience bound by Scripture cannot be unbound by statute.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern habit of filing every scruple about worship under personality — the high churchman likes ceremony, the low churchman does not, and both are served. Humphrey held that the question was not taste but authority: who may bind the worship of God, and on what warrant. Having lived in Zurich and seen a church ordered simply, he came back unable to pretend that the surplice was nothing.

The principle to recover is that conscience answers to God before it answers to the magistrate, and that this is not rebellion but the order of things. “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). The man who acts against his own judgment in worship is not thereby obedient: “for whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Rom 14:23). And the reward of such a course is not comfort but a clear testimony — “the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity” (2Co 1:12).

Usage

"“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the surplice refused at Oxford and the deprivation borne."

"“the testimony of our conscience” (2Co 1:12) — a scholar who had seen Zurich and would not unsee it."

"Magdalen filled with preachers under a President who thought England half-reformed."
